---

## 1. Narrative Arc

Over the six quarters in front of us, Yelp's story quietly changed shape — from "a resilient local-advertising machine throwing off cash" to "an advertising business in slow structural decline that is racing to reinvent itself with artificial intelligence."

In early 2025 (first quarter, call dated May 8, 2025) the headline was strength: 8% revenue growth, a Services advertising business compounding at double digits for a sixteenth straight quarter, and management leaning into a "product-led strategy." The weak spot — restaurants, retail and other categories, which the company calls "RR&O" — was framed as a temporary, macro-driven soft patch ("the operating environment... remain challenging").

By the second and third quarters of 2025, the tone shifted from confidence to caution. Growth decelerated to 4%, management stopped seeing the normal seasonal lift in advertiser budgets ("we did not see the seasonal increase in revenue that we would typically expect"), and they began lowering rather than raising the full-year outlook. The RR&O decline deepened.

By the fourth quarter of 2025 and especially the first quarter of 2026 (call dated May 8, 2026), the narrative had pivoted hard. The core advertising engine is now barely growing — Services advertising up just 1% and RR&O advertising down 11% year over year in the first quarter of 2026. In its place, management has elevated three new growth pillars to center stage: (1) "Yelp Assistant," an artificial-intelligence chatbot for getting service quotes; (2) two voice-answering software products, "Yelp Host" (for restaurants) and the Hatch acquisition (lead management for service pros); and (3) data licensing to AI search players, headlined by a newly announced OpenAI deal. The new banner metric is "other revenue," up 75% year over year, with a target to more than double it to a $250 million annual run rate by the end of 2028.

The arc, in plain terms: the old cash cow is fading, and management is spending the cash it throws off to buy back stock while planting AI seeds it hopes will replace the lost advertising growth.

|---|---|---|

| Services is the durable growth driver | Services advertising decelerated from +14% (Q1'25) to +8% (Q2'25) to +7% (Q3'25) to +1% (Q1'26) | Story is fading faster than management admits — the one healthy engine is now barely growing |
| Disciplined margins / margin potential | EBITDA margin slipped from 25% (FY2025) to 22% (Q1 2026); net income margin from 10% to 5%; net income **down 27%** YoY in Q1 2026 | Diverges sharply — margins are compressing, not holding |
| Free cash flow strength (FCF margin 22%) | TTM free cash flow $281M on ~$1.46B revenue — genuinely strong cash conversion | Confirmed — this is the real asset |

The central forensic finding: **the company's reported earnings-per-share growth has been manufactured by buying back stock and cutting stock-based compensation, not by the business getting bigger.** Revenue is nearly flat and the most profitable advertising lines are shrinking. The 2026 adjusted-EBITDA guide of $310–330M is a step *down* from the $369M delivered in 2025 — management is guiding to lower profit dollars even as it spends to grow.

---

## 3. Tone & Confidence Trajectory

**Declining.** The shift from offensive (growth, investment) to defensive (efficiency, macro, "challenging environment") language is unmistakable across the six calls.

- Q1 2025: confident, growth-forward — "continued strength," "16th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth."
- Q2 2025: first cracks — "advertisers exercised increased caution," "macroeconomic and policy uncertainties," budgets did not rise "to the same extent as we have seen historically."
- Q3 2025: defensive — lowered the full-year revenue range, ad clicks down 11%, leaned on cost discipline.
- Q4 2025 / Q1 2026: pivot mode — the calls became almost entirely about AI initiatives (Yelp Assistant, Yelp Host, Hatch, OpenAI), with the core advertising decline acknowledged but quickly redirected toward the new story. Guidance flagged "the degree of uncertainty that we need to reflect."

Management is becoming *less* specific about the core business (clicks, locations, RR&O) and *more* enthusiastic about early-stage AI products where there are no hard numbers to be held to yet. That is a classic tell of a management team steering attention away from a decelerating core.

---

## 4. Guidance Credibility

**High on the mechanics, low on the trajectory.** Yelp has a genuine habit of beating its own near-term guidance — the screener shows a 7-of-7 beat rate, and on each call adjusted EBITDA came in above the high end of the outlook range (e.g., Q1 2026 EBITDA was "$15 million above the high end"). This is real and earns credit.

---

Analysts circled the same wounds for six straight quarters:

- **The OpenAI / AI-search partnership reality.** A Bank of America analyst pressed directly in Q1 2026: "when I search for restaurants... on ChatGPT today, Yelp content appears relatively limited versus sources like Reddit, OpenTable, Tripadvisor." - **Hatch / AI-product scale and margin.** Analysts asked repeatedly how big and how profitable; management declined to quantify the contribution to next year, saying margin "is not the immediate focus."

---

🔴 **Core advertising decelerating to a stall** — Services advertising +1%, RR&O advertising -11% in Q1 2026; paying advertising locations down 6% to 485,000.
🔴 **Profit dollars guided down** — 2026 EBITDA guide $310–330M vs $369M actual in 2025; net income -27% YoY in Q1 2026.
🔴 **Falling engagement** — app unique devices down 2% YoY; ad clicks down 10–11% — the marketplace is being used less, propped up only by higher prices.
🔴 **The Google / AI existential question went unanswered** — management could not describe how its content actually shows up in ChatGPT or where it ranks versus rivals.
🔴 **Insider behavior** — open-market activity is zero buys versus 33 sells (~477,000 shares). No insider is putting cash in at these "cheap" prices.

🟢 **Exceptional free cash flow and a clean balance sheet** — $281M trailing free cash flow, only ~$45M net debt; 90% gross margins.
🟢 **Disciplined, aggressive, value-accretive buyback** — count cut ~22% in four years, buying heavily at $24–25, with a fresh $500M authorization. This directly compounds per-share value even with flat revenue.
🟢 **Stock-based compensation falling** — from ~10% to 8% of revenue, on track to under 6% by 2027, improving the *quality* of earnings.
🟢 **Real, if early, AI optionality** — Hatch growing ~90%, "other revenue" up 75%, genuine demand for data licensing from AI players. A free call option if it works.

---

## 7. Hidden Signals

- **The vocabulary flipped from "advertising" to "AI."** Early calls measured success in locations, clicks, and cost-per-click. Recent calls measure it in "features shipped" (35, then 55), "annual run rate" of calls handled, and partnership logos (Alexa, Apple Maps, Bing, Meta.ai, OpenAI). When a company stops quoting the metrics that pay the bills and starts quoting activity metrics, watch the core.
- **Capitalized software development is doing quiet work.** Management twice noted that more spending is being "capitalized" because of "greenfield projects" — this flatters near-term margins and EBITDA by pushing costs off the current income statement. A subtle quality-of-earnings caution.
- **The Hatch retention payments are added back to adjusted EBITDA** — management disclosed this directly. Adjusted EBITDA is being flattered by excluding real acquisition costs.
- **Capital allocation language subtly reordered.** Buybacks moved from the third priority to being framed alongside "strategic transactions" (the Hatch deal) — management is signaling it may spend more on acquisitions and less on buybacks going forward, which would remove the one reliable support under the per-share story.

---

## 8. Capital-Allocation Verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING — with a deteriorating core.** This is a company managing a slow structural decline in its advertising franchise by harvesting cash, shrinking the share count, and betting on artificial-intelligence products to eventually refill the growth tank. The buyback is excellent and the cash generation is real; the underlying business is eroding.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh:** Is the cheap price (about 4.8x free cash flow) a mispricing of a durable cash machine, or the market correctly pricing the slow death of a local-advertising business that Google's AI search and large language models are quietly disintermediating? The Q1 2026 numbers — Services advertising at +1%, the marketplace being used less each quarter, and management unable to explain how Yelp surfaces inside ChatGPT — tilt toward the second reading. The buyback can compound per-share value for a while even on a shrinking base, but it cannot reverse the secular tide.

**Economic moat:** an intangible-brand and content/network moat (330 million reviews, brand recognition in local search) that is **eroding**. The evidence is in the returns and margins: return on invested capital sits at ~9% (around or below a fair cost of capital for this risk), and although gross margin is a stable 90%, net margin halved (10% to 5%) and EBITDA margin fell (25% to 22%) in the most recent quarter, with clicks and engagement declining. A high gross margin on a shrinking, less-used marketplace is a melting asset, not a fortress.

**Secular threat — material, bordering on terminal.** The structural force is generative-AI displacement of search-and-discovery: Google holds roughly 73% of local-review share to Yelp's ~6%, about 68% of Google queries now end without a click to any outside site, and large language models like ChatGPT are becoming the new front door to local recommendations — with Yelp's own content showing up only "relatively limited" inside them. Yelp is trying to convert this threat into a data-licensing revenue stream, which is a smart hedge, but the base case is that AI search compresses the referral traffic Yelp's advertising model depends on. The cheapness is therefore better read as a structurally-shrinking base (a value-trap risk) partly offset by a strong buyback, not a clean fear-print.

**Declining.** The shift from offensive (growth, investment) to defensive (efficiency, macro, "challenging environment") language is unmistakable across the six calls.

**High on the mechanics, low on the trajectory.** Yelp has a genuine habit of beating its own near-term guidance — the screener shows a 7-of-7 beat rate, and on each call adjusted EBITDA came in above the high end of the outlook range (e.g., Q1 2026 EBITDA was "$15 million above the high end"). This is real and earns credit.

But there is a clear **sandbagging pattern**: they set conservative ranges, beat them, and book the applause — while the *full-year* numbers kept getting *cut* (the full-year revenue range was lowered in Q3 2025; 2026 EBITDA guidance of $310–330M is below 2025's actual $369M). Reliability of the quarter-ahead guide: **High.** Reliability of the multi-year growth narrative: **Low** — they have repeatedly described AI products as imminent revenue drivers without yet producing material revenue from them.

Analysts circled the same wounds for six straight quarters:

- **The OpenAI / AI-search partnership reality.** A Bank of America analyst pressed directly in Q1 2026: "when I search for restaurants... on ChatGPT today, Yelp content appears relatively limited versus sources like Reddit, OpenTable, Tripadvisor." - **What fixes RR&O?** Repeatedly asked; management consistently fell back on "it's a macro story" and "in-restaurant dining will return," deflecting the competitive-pressure framing (food-delivery players, Google) that analysts kept raising.

🟢 **Real, if early, AI optionality** — Hatch growing ~90%, "other revenue" up 75%, genuine demand for data licensing from AI players. A free call option if it works.

---

- **The vocabulary flipped from "advertising" to "AI."** Early calls measured success in locations, clicks, and cost-per-click. Recent calls measure it in "features shipped" (35, then 55), "annual run rate" of calls handled, and partnership logos (Alexa, Apple Maps, Bing, Meta.ai, OpenAI). When a company stops quoting the metrics that pay the bills and starts quoting activity metrics, watch the core.
- **Capitalized software development is doing quiet work.** Management twice noted that more spending is being "capitalized" because of "greenfield projects" — this flatters near-term margins and EBITDA by pushing costs off the current income statement. A subtle quality-of-earnings caution.
- **The Hatch retention payments are added back to adjusted EBITDA** — management disclosed this directly. Adjusted EBITDA is being flattered by excluding real acquisition costs.
- **Capital allocation language subtly reordered.** Buybacks moved from the third priority to being framed alongside "strategic transactions" (the Hatch deal) — management is signaling it may spend more on acquisitions and less on buybacks going forward, which would remove the one reliable support under the per-share story.

---

## 8. Capital-Allocation Verdict (for the director)

**Trajectory: PIVOTING — with a deteriorating core.** This is a company managing a slow structural decline in its advertising franchise by harvesting cash, shrinking the share count, and betting on artificial-intelligence products to eventually refill the growth tank. The buyback is excellent and the cash generation is real; the underlying business is eroding.

**The single most important thing the director must weigh:** Is the cheap price (about 4.8x free cash flow) a mispricing of a durable cash machine, or the market correctly pricing the slow death of a local-advertising business that Google's AI search and large language models are quietly disintermediating? The Q1 2026 numbers — Services advertising at +1%, the marketplace being used less each quarter, and management unable to explain how Yelp surfaces inside ChatGPT — tilt toward the second reading. The buyback can compound per-share value for a while even on a shrinking base, but it cannot reverse the secular tide.

**Economic moat:** an intangible-brand and content/network moat (330 million reviews, brand recognition in local search) that is **eroding**. The evidence is in the returns and margins: return on invested capital sits at ~9% (around or below a fair cost of capital for this risk), and although gross margin is a stable 90%, net margin halved (10% to 5%) and EBITDA margin fell (25% to 22%) in the most recent quarter, with clicks and engagement declining. A high gross margin on a shrinking, less-used marketplace is a melting asset, not a fortress.

**Secular threat — material, bordering on terminal.** The structural force is generative-AI displacement of search-and-discovery: Google holds roughly 73% of local-review share to Yelp's ~6%, about 68% of Google queries now end without a click to any outside site, and large language models like ChatGPT are becoming the new front door to local recommendations — with Yelp's own content showing up only "relatively limited" inside them. Yelp is trying to convert this threat into a data-licensing revenue stream, which is a smart hedge, but the base case is that AI search compresses the referral traffic Yelp's advertising model depends on. The cheapness is therefore better read as a structurally-shrinking base (a value-trap risk) partly offset by a strong buyback, not a clean fear-print.

# Forensic Dossier — Yelp Inc. (YELP)

*Prepared for the investment committee. Eight quarterly earnings calls reviewed (Q1 2025 through Q1 2026), cross-referenced against the screener's financial trajectory and a live balance-sheet and consensus pull as of 2026-07-10. Yelp is a local-business reviews and local-advertising platform: consumers discover restaurants and service pros; small businesses pay to advertise against that intent.*

## 1. NARRATIVE ARC

Over the last five quarters the story has quietly but decisively changed shape. In early 2025 the headline was **"services is carrying us."** Yelp had split its advertising base into two halves — Services (home and auto pros: plumbers, contractors, repair shops) and Restaurants, Retail & Other ("RR&O") — and Services was compounding at double digits (14% year-over-year in the first quarter of 2025, a sixteenth straight quarter of double-digit growth) while RR&O was shrinking. Management's message was that the strong half would outgrow the weak half and the blend would stay healthy.

That blend has since broken down. Services growth decelerated every quarter — 14% (Q1 2025) to 8% (Q2) to 7% (Q3) to roughly 1% (Q1 2026) — while RR&O's decline deepened from −3% to −11%. By the first quarter of 2026 total revenue grew just 1%. As the ad engine stalled, management pivoted the narrative hard toward **AI in two directions at once**: (1) AI-native new products — Yelp Assistant (an AI chatbot for getting quotes), Yelp Host and Yelp Receptionist (AI call-answering), and the February 2026 acquisition of Hatch (AI lead-management, growing ~92%); and (2) **data licensing** — selling Yelp's 330 million reviews and 8 million business listings to AI search players, culminating in a signed agreement with OpenAI and content appearing on Apple Maps, Amazon Alexa, Microsoft Bing and Meta.ai. The new rallying cry, repeated by the first quarter of 2026, is a target of a **$250 million annual run-rate in "other revenue" by the end of 2028** — more than double today's level.

So the arc is a company managing the slow erosion of its legacy advertising franchise by re-tooling around AI — partly as defense (its content is what AI search needs) and partly as offense (new SaaS lines). Growth drivers introduced: Yelp Assistant, Host, Hatch, licensing. Quietly de-emphasized: the old promise that Services growth alone would keep the top line healthy.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The numbers | Verdict |

| "Record net revenue," "strong profitability" | 2025 revenue $1.46B, up just 4%; Q1 2026 up 1% to $361M | **Poorer than it sounds** — records are set on 1–4% growth; the top line is effectively flat |

*Prepared for the investment committee. Over the last five quarters the story has quietly but decisively changed shape. Management's message was that the strong half would outgrow the weak half and the blend would stay healthy.

That blend has since broken down. Services growth decelerated every quarter — 14% (Q1 2025) to 8% (Q2) to 7% (Q3) to roughly 1% (Q1 2026) — while RR&O's decline deepened from −3% to −11%. By the first quarter of 2026 total revenue grew just 1%. As the ad engine stalled, management pivoted the narrative hard toward **AI in two directions at once**: (1) AI-native new products — Yelp Assistant (an AI chatbot for getting quotes), Yelp Host and Yelp Receptionist (AI call-answering), and the February 2026 acquisition of Hatch (AI lead-management, growing ~92%); and (2) **data licensing** — selling Yelp's 330 million reviews and 8 million business listings to AI search players, culminating in a signed agreement with OpenAI and content appearing on Apple Maps, Amazon Alexa, Microsoft Bing and Meta.ai. The new rallying cry, repeated by the first quarter of 2026, is a target of a **$250 million annual run-rate in "other revenue" by the end of 2028** — more than double today's level.

So the arc is a company managing the slow erosion of its legacy advertising franchise by re-tooling around AI — partly as defense (its content is what AI search needs) and partly as offense (new SaaS lines). Growth drivers introduced: Yelp Assistant, Host, Hatch, licensing. Quietly de-emphasized: the old promise that Services growth alone would keep the top line healthy.

## 2. CLAIMS vs FINANCIALS (forensic)

| Management claim | The numbers | Verdict |
|---|---|---|
| "Record net revenue," "strong profitability" | 2025 revenue $1.46B, up just 4%; Q1 2026 up 1% to $361M | **Poorer than it sounds** — records are set on 1–4% growth; the top line is effectively flat |

| Healthy balance sheet, capacity for deals | As of 2026-03-31: cash $110M, drew $130M long-term debt, ~$45M **net debt** (≈$20M ex-lease) | **Verified, with a correction** — the old "$300M net cash" is gone; Hatch + buybacks turned a net-cash balance sheet net-debt in one quarter |

The through-line: every favorable claim is *technically true* but sits on a top line that has gone flat, an engagement base that is shrinking, and a 2026 in which earnings actually fall. **Trajectory: Stable-to-defensive.** Management's tone is remarkably consistent and composed across all eight calls — no panic, no defensiveness, steady delivery. But the *content* shifted from offense to a mix of offense-and-defense:

- Q2 2025 (first hedge): advertisers "exercised increased caution," "we did not see the seasonal increase in revenue that we would typically expect."
- Q3 2025 (defensive on the core, offensive on AI): "heightened macroeconomic uncertainties will persist," lowered full-year revenue outlook — while touting "more than 35 new features" and Yelp Host.

Guidance became *more* specific over time (they now give quarterly revenue and adjusted-EBITDA ranges and 2028 run-rate targets), which is a confidence tell, but the specificity is increasingly about the new AI lines rather than the core ad business.

**Reliability: High.** This is management's strongest suit. Across the reviewed quarters they consistently guided conservatively and beat — the screener records a 7-of-7 earnings-beat rate. Three questions recur and management cannot yet answer them with numbers:

1. **"Is AI a net threat or opportunity?"** Bank of America's analyst pressed directly in Q1 2026: when you search restaurants on ChatGPT today, "Yelp content appears relatively limited versus sources like Reddit, OpenTable, Tripadvisor… what needs to happen for Yelp to become more visible?" 🔴 **Paying advertising locations falling** — 517,000 → 485,000 over five quarters (−6% YoY in Q1 2026); the customer count is eroding across *both* segments now, not only RR&O.
🔴 **Earnings actually decline in 2026** — net income −27% YoY in Q1; consensus EPS $2.24 → ~$1.88.
🔴 **Balance sheet flipped to net debt** — $130M drawn for Hatch, net cash gone; capital-allocation optionality reduced.
🔴 **Insiders: zero open-market buys against 34 sells (476,696 shares)** — no personal conviction at these "cheap" prices; the buyback is corporate, not personal.
🔴 **Gross margin slipping** (~90% → ~85%) as the revenue mix diversifies into lower-margin lines.

🟢 **Free cash flow is enormous and real** — ~$281M trailing, a ~20% free-cash-flow yield; this is not a cash-burning turnaround.
🟢 **Buyback is aggressive and accretive** — ~11% of shares retired in two quarters, ~22% over four years; at a ~20% FCF yield each dollar of repurchase is highly value-additive.
🟢 **Other revenue +75%** with genuine AI monetization (OpenAI licensing signed, Hatch +92%, DoorDash food-ordering +88%) — the pivot is producing measurable dollars.
🟢 **Guidance credibility is high** (7/7 beats, transparent sandbagging).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **The CPC-for-clicks trade is the tell.** Management has re-cast falling volume ("fewer clicks") as a feature ("higher-quality leads, higher CPC"). Revenue held because price offset volume. This is the classic late-stage move of a network whose usage is maturing — it can mask erosion for several quarters but not indefinitely.
- **"Other revenue" is being promoted from footnote to headline.** The 2028 run-rate target and the reclassification of DoorDash economics into "other revenue" signal management knows the ad line alone will not carry the story — they are re-basing investor attention onto the diversification.
- **The Hatch acquisition changed the capital-allocation posture.** For years the message was buyback-first with a net-cash balance sheet. Drawing debt to buy Hatch and explicitly saying margin is "not the immediate focus" for it is a real shift from harvesting to reinvesting — a bet that the AI-SaaS lines are worth more than the buyback they partly displaced.

## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING.** Yelp is re-tooling a maturing local-advertising franchise around AI — defensively (licensing its content to the very AI players that could disintermediate it) and offensively (Assistant, Host, Hatch). The legacy ad base is eroding at the edges (clicks, devices, locations, RR&O all down), but the company throws off a ~20% free-cash-flow yield and is shrinking the share count aggressively, so per-share value can compound even at zero top-line growth.

If licensing plus Services advertising plus the new SaaS lines stabilize the base, the stock is a ~5x-free-cash-flow mispricing. If consumer traffic keeps eroding and the new lines stay sub-scale, it is a cheap-looking melting asset.

**Economic moat: NARROW, and ERODING.** The moat is an intangible-content-plus-network asset — 330 million reviews, ~500 million photos, 8 million listings that competitors cannot cheaply replicate, proven valuable by the fact that OpenAI, Apple and Amazon license it. But it was always the number-two gateway to local search behind Google, and returns-quality is holding (return on invested capital ~15%, return on equity ~20%, gross margin still high) even as the *usage base* underneath shrinks. High-but-stable returns on a slowly-shrinking traffic base is the signature of a narrow moat being eroded, not a wide one.

**Secular threat: MATERIAL (not yet terminal).** The structural force is generative-AI displacement of "good-enough" discovery — the risk that consumers get local answers from an AI assistant without ever visiting Yelp, collapsing the ad impressions that are ~90% of revenue. It is *material* rather than *terminal* because (a) local-services advertising still depends on lead-generation and job completion that pure chat does not yet do, (b) Yelp's content is valuable enough that the AI platforms pay to license it, giving Yelp a second monetization path, and (c) the fast-growing other-revenue line is a genuine, if partial, offset. The cheapness is therefore a **fear-print with a real thorn in it** — not a pure mispricing, but not (yet) a pure value trap either. Size it as a watch-and-accumulate value name, not an aggressive-entry catalyst play.

🟢 **Other revenue +75%** with genuine AI monetization (OpenAI licensing signed, Hatch +92%, DoorDash food-ordering +88%) — the pivot is producing measurable dollars.
🟢 **Guidance credibility is high** (7/7 beats, transparent sandbagging).

- **The CPC-for-clicks trade is the tell.** Management has re-cast falling volume ("fewer clicks") as a feature ("higher-quality leads, higher CPC"). Revenue held because price offset volume. This is the classic late-stage move of a network whose usage is maturing — it can mask erosion for several quarters but not indefinitely.
- **"Other revenue" is being promoted from footnote to headline.** The 2028 run-rate target and the reclassification of DoorDash economics into "other revenue" signal management knows the ad line alone will not carry the story — they are re-basing investor attention onto the diversification.
- **The Hatch acquisition changed the capital-allocation posture.** For years the message was buyback-first with a net-cash balance sheet. **Classification: PIVOTING.** Yelp is re-tooling a maturing local-advertising franchise around AI — defensively (licensing its content to the very AI players that could disintermediate it) and offensively (Assistant, Host, Hatch). **Economic moat: NARROW, and ERODING.** The moat is an intangible-content-plus-network asset — 330 million reviews, ~500 million photos, 8 million listings that competitors cannot cheaply replicate, proven valuable by the fact that OpenAI, Apple and Amazon license it. The cheapness is therefore a **fear-print with a real thorn in it** — not a pure mispricing, but not (yet) a pure value trap either. Size it as a watch-and-accumulate value name, not an aggressive-entry catalyst play.

Over the last five quarters the story has quietly but decisively changed shape. In early 2025 the headline was **"services is carrying us."** Yelp had split its advertising base into two halves — Services (home and auto pros: plumbers, contractors, repair shops) and Restaurants, Retail & Other ("RR&O") — and Services was compounding at double digits (14% year-over-year in the first quarter of 2025, a sixteenth straight quarter of double-digit growth) while RR&O was shrinking. Management's message was that the strong half would outgrow the weak half and the blend would stay healthy.

That blend has since broken down. Services growth decelerated every quarter — 14% (Q1 2025) to 8% (Q2) to 7% (Q3) to roughly 1% (Q1 2026) — while RR&O's decline deepened from −3% to −11%. By the first quarter of 2026 total revenue grew just 1%. As the ad engine stalled, management pivoted the narrative hard toward **AI in two directions at once**: (1) AI-native new products — Yelp Assistant (an AI chatbot for getting quotes), Yelp Host and Yelp Receptionist (AI call-answering), and the February 2026 acquisition of Hatch (AI lead-management, growing ~92%); and (2) **data licensing** — selling Yelp's 330 million reviews and 8 million business listings to AI search players, culminating in a signed agreement with OpenAI and content appearing on Apple Maps, Amazon Alexa, Microsoft Bing and Meta.ai. The new rallying cry, repeated by the first quarter of 2026, is a target of a **$250 million annual run-rate in "other revenue" by the end of 2028** — more than double today's level.

## 3. TONE & CONFIDENCE TRAJECTORY

**Trajectory: Stable-to-defensive.** Management's tone is remarkably consistent and composed across all eight calls — no panic, no defensiveness, steady delivery. But the *content* shifted from offense to a mix of offense-and-defense:

- Q1 2025 (offense): "continued strength… strong profitability," Services "16th consecutive quarter of double-digit growth."
- Q2 2025 (first hedge): advertisers "exercised increased caution," "we did not see the seasonal increase in revenue that we would typically expect."
- Q3 2025 (defensive on the core, offensive on AI): "heightened macroeconomic uncertainties will persist," lowered full-year revenue outlook — while touting "more than 35 new features" and Yelp Host.

**Reliability: High.** This is management's strongest suit. Across the reviewed quarters they consistently guided conservatively and beat — the screener records a 7-of-7 earnings-beat rate. Three questions recur and management cannot yet answer them with numbers:

1. **"Is AI a net threat or opportunity?"** Bank of America's analyst pressed directly in Q1 2026: when you search restaurants on ChatGPT today, "Yelp content appears relatively limited versus sources like Reddit, OpenTable, Tripadvisor… what needs to happen for Yelp to become more visible?" 2. **"How big is the AI revenue, really, and when?"** Analysts repeatedly ask for the scale and timing of Yelp Host and Hatch. Management offers a "$1 billion+ TAM" and "$250M other-revenue run-rate by 2028" but declines to size near-term contribution.

🟢 **Other revenue +75%** with genuine AI monetization (OpenAI licensing signed, Hatch +92%, DoorDash food-ordering +88%) — the pivot is producing measurable dollars.
🟢 **Guidance credibility is high** (7/7 beats, transparent sandbagging).

## 7. HIDDEN SIGNALS

- **The CPC-for-clicks trade is the tell.** Management has re-cast falling volume ("fewer clicks") as a feature ("higher-quality leads, higher CPC"). Revenue held because price offset volume. This is the classic late-stage move of a network whose usage is maturing — it can mask erosion for several quarters but not indefinitely.
- **"Other revenue" is being promoted from footnote to headline.** The 2028 run-rate target and the reclassification of DoorDash economics into "other revenue" signal management knows the ad line alone will not carry the story — they are re-basing investor attention onto the diversification.
- **The Hatch acquisition changed the capital-allocation posture.** For years the message was buyback-first with a net-cash balance sheet. ## 8. CAPITAL-ALLOCATION VERDICT (for the director)

**Classification: PIVOTING.** Yelp is re-tooling a maturing local-advertising franchise around AI — defensively (licensing its content to the very AI players that could disintermediate it) and offensively (Assistant, Host, Hatch).
